summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Officials may not enter a home or seize a child without prior judicial authorization unless they possess information at the time of seizure establishing reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury, and the intrusion must be no broader than necessary to avert that injury.
key_cases.relevance: Accepting a report for investigation does not authorize entry or seizure absent this showing.
key_cases.quote: reasonable cause to believe that the child is in imminent danger of serious bodily injury and that the scope of the intrusion is reasonably necessary to avert that specific injury.

key_cases.case_name: Capp v. County of San Diego
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: A social worker who threatens to terminate a parent's custody in retaliation for the parent's protected criticism of the agency violates the First Amendment, and is not entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: The decision to open or expand an investigation may not be made in retaliation for protected speech.
key_cases.quote: A reasonable official would have known that taking the serious step of threatening to terminate a parent's custody of his children

timeline_requirements.deadline: As part of an investigation initiated pursuant to NRS 432B.260 the agency must determine, first in the order of priority set by the rule, whether the child is safe considering the factors set forth in NAC 432B.160; no separate deadline is set for that determination (NAC 432B.150(2)). The child must be seen immediately if the allegations suggest imminent harm (NAC 432B.150(3)(b)), and where the investigation was initiated by telephone or a review of a case record a face-to-face meeting with the child and his family must be attempted on the next business day and on each successive business day until the supervisor of the case manager of the case determines that a resolution has been achieved (NAC 432B.155(1))
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Investigation initiated by the agency which provides child welfare services pursuant to NRS 432B.260
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in NAC 432B.150 or NAC 432B.155
